Acțiune Facebook X WhatsApp Telegram VK Nearly half a billion Romanian lei managed in a single year, more than 1,400 hospital beds, almost 46,000 discharged patients and a staffing shortage affecting nearly every professional category. These are just some of the figures that define the Bacău County Emergency Hospital, the largest healthcare facility in Bacău County and one of the most important hospitals in Romania’s northeastern Moldavia region. The hospital’s 2025 activity report offers a snapshot of an institution operating close to capacity, handling a growing volume of patients while facing increasing challenges. 1. A Hospital the Size of a Small Neighborhood Bacău County Emergency Hospital has 1,449 approved beds , of which 1,341 are funded under contracts with Romania’s National Health Insurance House (CNAS) . It is the largest inpatient medical facility in the county. 2. Around 1,000 Patients Are Hospitalized Every Day Acute care wards recorded an average occupancy rate of 77.8% , while chronic care units operated at 66.8% occupancy. In practical terms, nearly 1,000 patients are hospitalized at the same time on any given day —roughly equivalent to the population of a small rural community. 3. One in Every 13 County Residents Is Hospitalized Here Each Year In 2025, the hospital treated and discharged 45,663 acute-care patients , in addition to more than 1,600 chronic-care cases . Relative to Bacău County’s population, this means that approximately one in every 13 residents is hospitalized at the facility each year , excluding patients referred from other counties. 4. Nearly One Quarter of Positions Remain Vacant The hospital’s staffing plan provides for 2,554 positions , but only 1,906 are currently filled . In other words, almost one out of every four positions is vacant , affecting virtually every professional category, from physicians and nurses to orderlies and support staff. 5. Nearly 100 Doctors Are Missing The hospital has 313 physician positions , yet only 220 are occupied . With a staffing rate of just 70% , the shortage places significant pressure on medical personnel and complicates the organization of emergency and on-call services. 6. The Largest Shortages Are Among Pharmacists and Orderlies While nursing positions are filled at a rate exceeding 80%, shortages are more severe in other essential areas. Only four of ten pharmacist positions are occupied, while just 22 of 37 orderly positions are filled. Although less visible to patients, these roles are essential to the hospital’s day-to-day operations. 7. Two-Thirds of the Hospital’s Budget Goes to Salaries In 2025, the hospital reported total revenues of 465.6 million lei . Of that amount, 307.3 million lei—66% of total revenue—was spent on personnel costs . The figures illustrate a common reality across public healthcare systems: medical services depend primarily on human resources. 8. Medicines Cost More Than 63 Million Lei Per Year After salaries, pharmaceuticals represent the hospital’s largest expenditure. In 2025, spending on medicines reached 63.7 million lei , accounting for nearly 14% of total revenue . Additional costs include medical supplies, laboratory reagents and disinfectants, all indispensable to patient care. 9. Patients Are Becoming Increasingly Complex The hospital’s Case Mix Index (CMI) —an indicator used to measure the complexity of treated cases—increased from 1.55 in 2024 to 1.62 in 2025 . Although the increase appears modest, it reflects a growing number of patients requiring more advanced diagnostics, procedures and medical resources. 10. Day Hospital Services Continue to Expand One encouraging trend is the increasing use of day hospitalization. The hospital delivered 105% of its contracted day-care services , indicating that a growing number of examinations and treatments can be performed without overnight admission. This reflects the direction taken by modern healthcare systems, which increasingly emphasize efficient treatment, shorter hospital stays and lower costs. Conclusion The 2025 activity report portrays a hospital operating under constant pressure. Bacău County Emergency Hospital treats tens of thousands of patients every year, manages a budget approaching half a billion lei , and handles increasingly complex medical cases. At the same time, staffing shortages remain its greatest challenge. Nearly 650 positions are vacant , including almost 100 physician posts , placing sustained pressure on the existing workforce. The paradox is clear: despite filling only about 75% of its approved staffing positions , personnel expenses already account for two-thirds of the hospital’s revenue . The hospital’s future will therefore depend not only on recruiting additional healthcare professionals, but also on securing sustainable funding and improving efficiency while meeting the growing healthcare needs of the population. https://www.bordermail.com.au/story/9322.text: Victim fearing for his life after armed home invasion, 'gunman' back in custody A man on bail over an alleged armed home invasion involving a 3D-printed firearm has been rearrested after allegedly fleeing police in another person's car. Subscribe now for unlimited access. Login or signup to continue reading Jake Reid Macklan is accused of entering the victim's Warsaw Crescent home in Wodonga with another unknown man on February 16. The Wodonga court heard the victim's front door was kicked in and he fled to a laundry. He was cornered by the unknown man and was punched 20 times and kicked in his testicles. When he fell over, Macklan allegedly pointed a black .22-calibre printed handgun at the victim and said "I told you this would happen, you need to learn a lesson". The unknown intruder hit him with a broom, breaking it, before the victim said "I'm done, I'm done". The unknown man smashed a television on the way out. The victim said Macklan was a drug dealer, and he owed Macklan $200. He was arrested in a vehicle on Melbourne Road on February 19, with 65 grams of marijuana and 2.2 grams of what appeared to be methamphetamine seized. Macklan gave a Strathmore Street address as his home, but a search of the property was unable to find any firearms. The victim reported that Macklan had four pistols before the incident. Macklan was bailed on March 20 but handed himself in at the Wodonga station following a recent incident. Detective Leading Senior Constable Tracy Jarrott said NSW officers were conducting breath tests on Wednesday, July 29. Macklan pulled up in a vehicle not owned by him and gave a digital licence which was suspended. Police noticed a strong smell of cannabis and went to search the vehicle. The court heard Macklan drove forward when officers tried to open the car door and sped off, hitting a gutter. Officers pursued the vehicle but were unable to catch it. Police spoke to him and he agreed to hand himself in on Thursday, July 30. Macklan had been bailed to a home at Kialla, but Detective Leading Senior Constable Jarrott was concerned about him mixing in old circles in Albury-Wodonga. "It's serious offending that he's currently on bail for," she said. "I have concerns about him having access to those guns. "This incident was all over a $200 drug debt. "If you're willing to smash on someone's door, go in, threaten them, assault them, point a firearm at them for $200 ... there's always that possibility of retribution. "It's definitely a concern." The court heard the victim was "scared for his life and what the accused may do next time". Macklan's bail application will return to court on Monday, August 3. https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/hungary-energy.text: Hungarians are bracing for blackouts as the Paks Nuclear Power Plant was shut down amid the European heatwave. Paks, which supplies almost half of the country's electricity, had to stop generating power because of record-low water levels in the Danube River, which is essential for cooling the plant.'Due to the further drop in the Danube's water level, one of the last two generating units at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant will be shut down at 1:30 a.m.,' announced Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar on his social media accounts. 'As a result, the plant's output will fall to just 240 megawatts, and tomorrow it will be completely shut down for the first time in 44 years.'Why the Danube River Is Essential for Power SupplyThe Danube River flows through and benefits 10 countries. It has receded to historic lows as Europe continues to grapple with the seemingly never-ending heat dome. Some parts of the body of water have even exposed the riverbed, while others have exposed old shipwrecks, artifacts, and fossils.The Danube is essential for cooling operations at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant. The plant siphons water directly from the river to cool down its reactors. But the European heatwave dropped water levels to unprecedented lows that the plant's suction equipment could no longer reach the water.Last week, Budapest energy officials recorded water levels at 23 centimeters (nine inches), which is much lower than the previous lowest-level record of 33 centimeters (13 inches) set in 2018. Magyar said the next five days will be critical to Hungary's energy situation.Moderate Use of Electricity'The government, together with energy and water management experts, evaluated the expected consumption data for tomorrow and the week ahead, the available domestic power plant capacities, and the expected import and trading opportunities for tomorrow. Mandatory restrictions on household consumption will not be necessary,' Magyar also announced.While there will be no mandatory load shedding yet, government officials have asked major consumer companies to voluntarily reduce the use of power. Hungarian citizens were also asked to use energy moderately, especially during the 'critical period' between 5 p.m. and 10 p.m.The European Commission is also contemplating meeting the Electricity Coordination Group to discuss Hungary's power problem. 'Although the operator has emergency measures in place to guarantee nuclear safety, an event of this kind could further strain the regional electricity balance,' European Commission spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said. 'The Commission stands ready to convene an ad hoc meeting of the Electricity Coordination Group.'Decentralised Energy System MulledEnvironmentalists believe this is a signal for Hungary to think of better energy distribution in the nation. 'Hungary needs to speed up its transition into a more resilient, decentralised energy system that relies less on climate-vulnerable infrastructure and more on energy savings, flexibility and renewable energy,' said Akos Eger, executive president of Friends of the Earth Hungary.Another climate organisation, Energiaklub, believes the situation is a serious test on Hungary's regional power supply. 'From Monday, when consumption is expected to rise and the Paks plant remains offline, a more serious situation will begin,' said András Perger, who believes that Hungary will stand to lose 25% to 30% of its energy output due to the shutdown.

http://www.europesun.com/news/279344887/.text: Baltic states PM trashes NATO Russian threat claim RT.com 01 Oct 2026, 05:38 GMT+10 Mindaugas Sinkevicius has warned against exaggerating the threat of an imminent conflict with Moscow Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius has said there is no evidence that Russia is preparing an attack on NATO territory, following a meeting with the military bloc's chief, Mark Rutte, in Brussels. His remarks came amid heightened tensions between Russia and NATO, as some Western officials and intelligence agencies have warned that Moscow could be preparing operations against member states in Europe. At a press conference on Tuesday, an AFP reporter asked Sinkevicius, whose Baltic country borders Russia's Kaliningrad exclave and Moscow's close ally Belarus, whether the "increasing hysteria and fear of hybrid attacks" could undermine Europe's confidence and play into Russia's hands. "We're not shaking. We're not shivering. We are investing hugely in our defense capabilities," Sinkevicius replied. "I think it's a must to say if the threat is there for the society. But you can't exaggerate and say, 'Oh, something is happening in the upcoming months or weeks,'" he added. "I was addressing the secretary general [Rutte, asking] 'Is there any proof, real proof intelligence services are providing, something on the table, that Russia is getting ready for something?' And there is actually none," Sinkevicius said. "The risk remains but it is not fluctuating, increasing or decreasing. We have to calmly do our work, and we're doing it," he added. His comments were also reported contemporaneously by international media. Rutte said the bloc should respond to potential threats by strengthening its own defenses and doing "even more for Ukraine, and not less." Speaking at the Euronews Defence & Space Summit in Brussels the following day, the NATO chief similarly sought to play down fears of an imminent Russian attack. "There is no imminent threat to NATO territory. If there is a build-up, we will see it and we will deal with it," Rutte said. European officials have increasingly discussed the possibility of a military confrontation with Russia, particularly around Kaliningrad, which is sandwiched between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kstutis Budrys argued in May that NATO must demonstrate its ability to "break into" the Russian exclave and destroy its air-defense and missile systems if necessary. Polish Foreign Minister Radosaw Sikorski said last month that NATO members should closely monitor Russian forces in Kaliningrad and conduct exercises "so aggressively" that Moscow would be forced to divert troops from Ukraine to defend the region. The Kremlin has described remarks about Kaliningrad as "borderline crazy," while the Russian Embassy in Belgium condemned what it called "an unprecedented surge" in NATO military activity along Russia's western borders. "The Alliance is conducting a large-scale information campaign to propagate the myth of the 'Russian threat' and spread false information about Moscow's alleged 'intentions' to attack one of the Baltic states by 2029 at the latest, or even sooner," the Russian Embassy said on X on Monday. It warned NATO members that "reckless and irresponsible" actions risked triggering a direct armed conflict. https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/actualitate/.text: Un liceu din centrul Craiovei a fost evacuat după ce o conductă de gaze a fost spartă de muncitori. La fața locului intervin angajați ai distribuitorului de gaze, pompieri și polițiști. ACTUALIZARE 10.15 Din primele informații, conducta a fost spartă din greșeală de muncitorii care reparau gardul liceului. A fost evacuată și o grădiniță din zonă, deoarece nu mai poate fi încălzită și nu mai poate fi pregătită mâncarea pentru copii, în condițiile în care gazele au fost oprite. Autoritățile speră ca în cursul zilei de astăzi să fie remediată această problemă și de mâine să fie reluate cursurile în condiții normale. Știrea inițială: „În aceste momente, intervenim în zona Liceului «Petrache Trişcu» din municipiul Craiova, în urma fisurării unei conducte de gaze, ca urmare a unor lucrări efectuate cu un buldoexcavator. La faţa locului se intervine cu o autospecială de lucru cu apă şi spumă şi o autospecială CBRN. Pentru prevenirea producerii unor situaţii de urgenţă, pompierii au balizat şi delimitat zona, iar preventiv au dispus evacuarea elevilor din şase săli de clasă, aproximativ 200 de elevi şi 30 de cadre didactice”, a anunţat ISU Dolj. De asemenea, autoritățile au închis strada pe care se află acest liceu. A fost oprită alimentarea cu gaze în zonă pentru a evita o explozie. Urmărește știrile Digi24.ro și pe Google News

Unplugged with Amantha Perera Level Up Down Under With Imran Sailbo World Focus FULL FRONTAL by Chandri Peris SCRIBBLES BY IMRAN SAIBO Previous Election Presidential Election General Election Life Cartoon Todays Exchange Rate Political Gossip Press Release Special Editions Infographics Fact check Poll Obituary Podcast Medicine Hard Talk Technology Insight Voice of People Archieve Daily FT Sunday Times Mirror Edu Tamil Mirror Lankadeepa Middleast Lankadeepa Ada Deshaya Life Online Hi Online HitAd TimesJobs E-Paper Home delivery advertise-with-us Mobile Apps feedback Archive Print Ads WNL Home Home Breaking News Opinion Features Expose Business Sports World News Videos The Sun Life Obituaries Trending Breaking News Top Stories Dengue Tracker Home News Cartoon Life Opinion Podcast Sports Features Poland wants India to push Russia towards peace in Ukraine DW - During his recent visit to India, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk seemingly went out of his way to ingratiate himself to Narendra Modi, describing the Indian leader as a "beacon of hope" in the times of global uncertainty and instability. One of the issues the two prime ministers discussed was the war in Ukraine, a country bordering Poland which Warsaw supports diplomatically and militarily against Russia. "We will support all efforts aimed at achieving peace," Modi said during the joint press briefing. Previous reports indicated India had formulated a plan to halt strikes on energy infrastructure between Russia and Ukraine and protect ships transporting grain and fuel. Before traveling to New Delhi, Tusk had also indicated that India "could play a constructive role" regarding the war, saying that this aspect was "very important" to him. While no concrete steps were announced during his trip, many in Europe still hope India can use its friendship with Russia to boost peace talks. Analysts warn, however, that New Delhi's access to the Kremlin does not automatically grant it sway over Russian President Vladimir Putin and his decisions. India 'cannot guarantee peace' India is unlikely to sacrifice its own interests at Europe's insistence, says India's former ambassador to Poland Anil Wadhwa. So far, New Delhi has maintained its political and defense relationship with Moscow while calling for dialogue and diplomacy and resisting pressure to align fully with Western sanctions. Moreover, while New Delhi may be able to communicate with both Moscow and Kyiv, there is no guarantee either side will respond to its efforts or make concessions. "Poland wants India to use its access to Vladimir Putin to encourage a ceasefire and meaningful negotiations, while recognizing the limits of New Delhi's influence over Russian military decisions," he told DW. The challenge, Wadhwa said, was to translate India's diplomatic access into practical outcomes without expecting too much. "India can contribute to de-escalation and help create conditions for negotiations, but it cannot guarantee peace," he said. Europe moves closer to India despite Russia row The Polish initiative also reflects a wider European effort to deepen relations with India. Ummu Salma Bava, chairperson and Jean Monnet Chair at the Centre for European Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, told DW that Tusk's visit had two objectives: strengthening ties between India and his own country and persuading New Delhi to factor in the EU's perspective on the Ukraine war. "The Ukraine war has become central to European security. India's strong association with Moscow despite the war has raised concerns on developing cooperation on security between India and the EU," Bava said. Poland, a frontline state, does not want Russia to gain additional economic benefits from its relationship with India. So far, according to Bava, "both sides have managed to compartmentalize the Ukraine issue" while advancing cooperation on trade, security and defense. But their differences could complicate future efforts to expand defense and security cooperation, she warned. US shift on Ukraine lets EU allies change stance Ajay Bisaria, another former envoy to Poland, says India's position has "matured into that of a potential peacemaker" and its ability to communicate with both Kyiv and Moscow is now perceived as useful. According to Bisaria, not even Warsaw regards "the Russia question" as a "significant irritant in the India-Europe or India-Poland relationship." "Europe, and Poland in particular, understands the depth of India's partnership with Russia, just as India appreciates the very different lens through which much of Europe views Moscow and the war in Ukraine," Bisaria told DW.
